transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I came in because I’m just... I'm tired all the time. And I know I'm a teacher, so being tired kind of comes with the territory, but this isn't that normal teacher-at-the-end-of-the-day tired. It's like, even after a full night’s sleep, I have to completely push myself through grading, and making dinner, and... 

Actually, speaking of grading, the district just rolled out this new literacy curriculum this semester, and it is an absolute nightmare. They want us to do these individual assessments for every single kid, which takes forever, and the parents are already complaining because the worksheets look different. I had one mom, Mrs. Davis, corner me at drop-off yesterday to argue about sight words for twenty minutes. She just wouldn't let it go, and she brought her labradoodle with her, right onto the playground, which is completely against the school policy, but nobody ever enforces it. 

But anyway, yeah, I was just standing there thinking about how much I wanted to go back to bed. It's just... I have to force myself through all of it. Even just getting my things ready for the next morning feels like I'm moving through molasses.
Do you still find joy in activities that you used to enjoy, such as teaching or hobbies outside of work?

Well, most days I can still put on a smile for my students and get through the lessons. Like, we were doing fractions today, and I always use the little magnet pizza slices on the whiteboard because it actually keeps them engaged. Though honestly, the district changed the lunch menu this year and the cafeteria pizza is literally just cardboard now. I don't know why they switched vendors, probably budget cuts, but the kids just throw it away, which is such a terrible waste of food. 

But... where was I? Oh. Yeah, I smile and teach, but underneath it all, it just feels like there’s this constant gray, flat feeling. And it just sticks to me. It follows me all the way home. I used to really look forward to my hobbies, like my garden or doing watercolors. I actually have this really beautiful set of paints I bought when my sister visited from Oregon. We went to this tiny art supply shop downtown that smells exactly like cedar and old paper, it's such a great little store, the owner is this sweet older man who always gives out free brush samples. But lately... I don't know. Even the garden and my watercolors just seem so far away. I just look at them and that flat feeling is still there.
Are there any activities that you still enjoy and look forward to?

I mean... no, not really. I try to think of something I want to do, and I just draw a blank. Even on the weekends, I wake up and I just... I don't really want to do anything. Which reminds me, I actually need to go to the grocery store this weekend because I'm completely out of coffee, and I cannot start my week without it. I usually go to the Trader Joe's on 4th Street, but the parking lot there is just a complete nightmare. It's so small, and people drive like maniacs trying to get a spot. Last time I was there, this guy in a massive SUV almost backed right into my sedan, and he didn't even look over his shoulder. I had to honk my horn for like ten seconds straight before he stopped. It's just so stressful. I honestly don't know why they don't just expand the lot, there's that empty field right next to it that's been vacant for years... but anyway. No, I don't really have anything I look forward to right now. It's just all... exhausting.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

I mean, yeah, I think I just said that... it's all just kind of gone. The watercolors, the garden, everything. It's like someone just turned down the volume on my whole life. I used to spend hours out in the yard, especially in the spring. Oh, actually, my neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he just planted these massive hydrangea bushes right along our shared fence line. They're gorgeous, really, but they are totally going to block the morning sun from hitting my tomato plants once they grow in. I tried to casually mention it to him when he was out there with his trowel, but he's super hard of hearing and just smiled and waved at me. I feel bad because he's a sweet old guy, his wife passed away a few years ago, but I really don't want my tomatoes to suffer. They need at least six hours of direct sunlight, you know? But... yeah. I just don't have the energy to care about the tomatoes right now anyway. I just don't have interest in any of it anymore.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite lately?

No, not really. My appetite is pretty much the same as it's always been. I still eat three meals a day, though honestly, packing a lunch for school has become such a chore. I usually just throw a sandwich and an apple in my bag. Speaking of apples, one of my students, Leo, brought in this huge Honeycrisp apple for me yesterday. It was so sweet of him. His family owns an orchard out past the county line, and they do this big fall festival every year with a corn maze and hayrides. I went a couple of years ago with a friend, and we got so incredibly lost in that maze. We were wandering around for almost an hour, and it started getting dark, which was actually kind of spooky because the corn stalks were way taller than us. We ended up having to ask this teenager dressed as a scarecrow for directions out. It was embarrassing, but we laughed about it the whole way home. But anyway, yeah, I'm eating fine. Nothing's really changed with my appetite.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

No, not really. I sleep about the same as always. I usually just kind of pass out once I finish grading my last batch of papers for the night. Actually, I did just buy this new weighted blanket online because I heard they were supposed to be super cozy. Not that I needed help sleeping, but they had this huge flash sale. It finally arrived on Tuesday, but the delivery guy left it right out in the rain instead of putting it up on the covered part of the porch. The box was completely soaked through. I had to drag this heavy, wet cardboard mess into my hallway, and it left mud everywhere. I spent like twenty minutes scrubbing the floor with those Swiffer pads, which, by the way, really do not hold as much dirt as the commercials claim they do. I end up using like three or four of them just for the entryway. I should probably just buy a real mop at this point, but I never remember when I'm at the store. But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, sleep. Yeah, no, my sleep is totally fine.
Have you been feeling guilty or worthless about anything lately?

I mean... yeah. I just keep thinking I should be handling everything better, you know? Like, my lesson plans are taking me twice as long to get through lately. And I actually just had to say no to mentoring this newer teacher. Her name is Emily, she just moved here from Oregon. Apparently, it rains there even more than it does here, which I didn't think was possible. She brought in these fancy artisanal donuts for the staff lounge on her first day, like, maple bacon and lavender glazed. I tried the lavender one, and honestly, it just tasted like eating potpourri. I really don't get the whole floral food trend. My grandmother used to keep lavender sachets in her dresser drawers, and now whenever I smell it or taste it, I just think of mothballs and scratchy old cardigans. She had this massive collection of cardigans, all color-coordinated in her closet... but anyway, I just felt so bad saying no to Emily. I just keep telling myself I’m letting my school down, and letting my family down, because I just can't keep up with what I'm supposed to be doing. So, yeah, I guess I do feel a lot of guilt.
Have you been having any thoughts about hurting yourself?

No, no, I haven't had any thoughts like that. I'd never do that. I just... I don't know, I just keep pushing through, I guess. It's like how I keep pushing through the grading pile every weekend. I was actually grading this set of history dioramas last Sunday, and one kid, Mason, he made this incredible model of the Alamo out of sugar cubes. It was so detailed, but he didn't seal it or anything, and I guess we have ants in the classroom now? Because by Monday morning, there was this massive trail of them marching right up the side of his project. The custodian, Mr. Henderson, had to come in with this industrial spray, and it smelled awful, like lemons and chemicals. He's been working at the school for like thirty years, Mr. Henderson. He always wears these suspenders with little tools on them. He actually fixed my stapler last month when it jammed so badly I thought I was going to have to throw it away. I've had that stapler since my first year of teaching. It's this bright red Swingline, just like the one in that movie, you know? Office Space? I watched that movie with my brother years ago, and he laughed so hard he spilled his soda all over my couch. It took me forever to get the stain out. But anyway... no, no thoughts of hurting myself or anything like that. Just feeling a bit overwhelmed, I guess.
How long have you been feeling this way?

I mean, it feels like forever, honestly, but I guess it's been about two years and two months? Right around the time my husband stopped working outside the house. Our whole routine just completely flipped. He used to commute into the city, which meant he was out the door by 6:30 AM. He took the train, the one that stops right by that little bakery on 4th Street. They have the best almond croissants there. We used to go every Sunday morning before they started getting too popular and the line would wrap around the block. I can't stand waiting in lines, especially when it's cold out. Last winter, I waited for forty-five minutes at the post office just to mail a package to my sister in Florida. She wanted this specific brand of hot cocoa mix that she can't find down there, which is funny because who drinks hot cocoa in Florida? It’s like ninety degrees year-round. She says she blasts the AC and drinks it anyway, which just seems like a massive waste of electricity to me. Our electric bill was through the roof last month, actually. But yeah, anyway, the routine changed back then, and I've just been feeling this way since.
How often do you find yourself thinking that you're letting others down?

Well, it feels like it's all the time lately. I just... I keep thinking I should be handling everything better. Like I mentioned before, with the lesson plans taking twice as long, and having to tell Emily I couldn't mentor her. Every time something like that happens, I just tell myself I'm letting my family down, and I'm letting my school down. It's just a constant loop in my head. Especially when I'm sitting at the dining room table trying to grade papers. We bought that table at an estate sale a few years ago. It's this beautiful solid oak, but it has this one scratch on the corner that drives me crazy. The guy who sold it to us said it was from his golden retriever when it was a puppy. I always wanted a dog, but my husband is allergic. He gets these awful hives if he's even in the same room as a dog for too long. He had to take Benadryl at his cousin's wedding because they had this ring-bearer dog, a little pug wearing a tiny tuxedo. It was cute, I guess, but it kept trying to eat the flower petals off the aisle runner. The bride was so mad. She had these very specific white roses imported from somewhere in South America. They must have cost a fortune. I mean, spending that much on flowers just seems ridiculous to me, they just die in a few days anyway. I prefer potted plants, like succulents. They're so much harder to kill. I have three of them on my desk at school. But anyway, yeah, I just always feel like I'm not doing enough and I'm letting everyone down.
How often do you have thoughts that you're a failure or that you're worthless?

It's, um, it's pretty much a constant thing. Like I was saying a minute ago, I just keep thinking I should be handling everything better. When my lesson plans take twice as long to finish, or when I had to tell Emily I couldn't mentor her, I just tell myself I'm letting my family down, and my school down. It just makes me feel like a complete failure. Emily was so sweet about it, though. She brought me a coffee the next day from that new place that opened up near the mall. Have you been there? They have these little espresso beans covered in dark chocolate on top of the foam. It's so good, but it kept me up half the night because I drank it at like 3 PM. I usually try not to have caffeine after noon because otherwise I just lay in bed staring at the ceiling fan. Our ceiling fan makes this weird clicking noise on the medium setting. My husband tried to fix it last weekend, but he ended up dropping his screwdriver and it chipped the hardwood floor in the bedroom. We just got those floors refinished last summer, too. The contractor was this guy named Steve who talked a lot about his competitive bass fishing tournaments. He actually showed me pictures of this giant fish he caught in Lake Mead. It was huge, honestly kind of terrifying. I don't really like being out on the water. I get seasick so easily. We went on a cruise for our honeymoon to the Bahamas, and I spent the first two days just miserable in the cabin. But anyway... yeah, those thoughts about being worthless, they're just always there when I can't keep up with things like I used to.
Would you say that these feelings of worthlessness and failure are mild, moderate, or severe?

I guess I'd say they're mild, mostly? But they're just... always there, you know? Like I said, I just keep thinking I should be handling everything better. When I'm sitting there and the lesson plans are taking twice as long, or like when I had to tell Emily no about the mentoring... I just tell myself I'm letting my family down, letting the school down. Emily is doing okay, by the way. She actually wore this really bright yellow cardigan yesterday that I loved. I meant to ask her where she got it, but then the fire alarm went off. It was just a drill, thank goodness, but those drills are so chaotic with the younger kids. You have to keep them all in a straight line and quiet, which is basically impossible for fourth graders. One kid, Tommy, he always tries to sneak his trading cards out during drills. He has this massive binder of them. I used to collect stamps when I was his age. My grandfather would send me stamps from all over the world. He was in the Navy, so he traveled everywhere. He brought me back this beautiful wooden music box from Japan once. It plays this really sad, slow melody. I keep it on my dresser, but I don't wind it up much anymore because the spring is getting kind of rusty. I should probably try to clean it, but who has the time? I can barely get through my grading. But yeah... mild, I think. Just a constant mild feeling that I'm letting everyone down.
How long have you been feeling this constant gray, flat feeling that you mentioned earlier?

Well, let's see... I think it's been going on for about two years and two months now. Yeah, because it really started right around the time my husband stopped working outside the home and our whole household routine changed. He shifted to remote work, so we had to completely clear out the guest room to make him a home office. We had this huge, heavy sleeper sofa in there that we had to drag out to the curb. It was a nightmare. We actually bought that sofa from IKEA when we first got married. I remember putting it together, it took us like six hours and we ended up with three extra screws. Don't you hate that? When you finish building furniture and there are parts left over? It makes you feel like the whole thing is just going to collapse the second you sit on it. 

Anyway, we dragged it out for the bulk trash pickup, but it rained that night, so it just sat there getting completely soaked and heavy before the truck finally came. The garbage men looked so annoyed having to lift it. I felt terrible, I almost went out and offered them some Gatorade. I usually keep the blue Gatorade in the fridge, the glacier freeze one, because it's the only flavor my husband likes. He's so picky about drinks. He won't even drink tap water unless it's been through the Brita pitcher twice. It takes forever to filter, and I'm always the one who has to refill it because he just puts it back in the fridge empty. But yeah... about two years and two months of just feeling flat like this.
Would you describe your recent episodes of feeling down as mild, moderate, or severe?

I guess I'd say mild. Because most days, you know, I can still smile for my students and get through the lessons. We were actually doing watercolors in class on Tuesday, which is usually one of my favorite activities to do with them. We were painting landscapes, and this one little girl, Sarah, she accidentally spilled her entire cup of purple paint water all over her desk. It dripped down into her backpack and completely soaked her library book. It was that book about the mouse who rides a motorcycle? I loved that book when I was little. I used to read it under the covers with a flashlight because my mom wanted me asleep by 8:30 sharp. She was so strict about bedtimes, she would actually come in and check the temperature of my lamp to see if I had just turned it off. 

But anyway... yeah, I can get through the day and put on a good face, but underneath it just feels like there’s this gray, flat feeling. It just follows me home. And then when I'm finally there, it makes even my own garden or my own watercolors seem so far away. I haven't even watered my hydrangeas out front in days. They're starting to look all droopy and wilted. I bought them at this little nursery down on 4th street that has a resident cat. The cat is huge, this big orange tabby, and he just sleeps on the bags of potting soil all day. I tried to pet him once and he completely ignored me. Cats are so funny like that, they just do not care what you want. My aunt had a cat that would only drink water if it was running from the bathroom sink... but yeah, just a mild, flat feeling, mostly.
How long have you felt like you've lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

I'm not really sure, honestly. I don't know if I can pinpoint exactly when I stopped caring about my hobbies. It just sort of... faded out, I guess? Like with my gardening. I used to be out there every weekend, pulling weeds, pruning the rosebushes. We have these gorgeous climbing roses on the trellis by the garage. They're a deep crimson color. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she has pink ones, but I always thought the red looked more classic. Mrs. Gable is so sweet, though. She baked us a rhubarb pie last month when her sister came to visit. I didn't even know people still made rhubarb pie! It was a little tart for my taste, to be honest. My husband ate most of it. He loves anything with a crust. He even eats the crusts off his sandwiches, which I think is so weird. I always cut the crusts off my sandwiches when I was a kid. My mom used to get so mad at me for wasting food. She grew up with four brothers, so at their dinner table, if you didn't eat fast, you didn't eat at all. They would literally reach across the table and steal potatoes right off her plate. Can you imagine? But yeah... I don't really know how long it's been since I lost interest. Just a while, I suppose.
Would you say that your episodes of feeling down have been consistently mild over the past two years, or have there been times when they felt more severe?

I don't really know if they've always been mild... I mean, I guess it's just been this same flat feeling the whole time? It's hard to tell if it gets worse or not because it's just always there. Kind of like this hum in the background. Speaking of hums, our refrigerator has been making this awful buzzing sound for the last three weeks. It's driving me completely crazy. It only happens at night, right when I'm trying to grade papers at the kitchen table. I called the repair guy, and he said he couldn't come out until next Thursday between 8 AM and noon. Why do they always give you those huge windows? Like I'm just supposed to sit around my house for four hours waiting. I can't do that, I have to be at school. I teach third grade, I can't just tell my principal I'm staying home for a refrigerator repairman. 

My principal, Mr. Harrison, he's such a stickler for attendance. He actually gives out these little certificates at the end of the year to the teachers who don't take any sick days. It's so silly, we're adults, we don't need certificates. He prints them on this really cheap parchment paper that always jams the copier in the teachers' lounge. Last time it jammed, Mrs. Davis—she teaches fifth grade—she got toner all over her favorite white blouse. She was so upset, she had to wear her winter coat all day in the classroom just to hide the stain. And it was like 75 degrees outside. But anyway, yeah, I'm not really sure if the feeling gets more severe. It just feels like it's always just sort of... there. Mild, I guess.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in or look forward to doing?

I... well, I don't really think there's anything right now. I just can't think of anything I actually look forward to. Even the things I used to love just seem like too much work. Like baking. I used to bake every Sunday. I'd make these huge batches of chocolate chip cookies for the teachers' lounge on Mondays. I always used the recipe on the back of the yellow bag of chocolate chips, but I'd add a little extra vanilla extract. My grandmother taught me that trick. She used to make her own vanilla extract by soaking vanilla beans in vodka for months in this dark glass bottle she kept in the back of her pantry. It smelled so strong, like alcohol and sugar. Her pantry was always full of the most interesting things. She had these old metal tins from the 1950s that she kept flour and sugar in. One of them had a picture of a rooster on it, and the lid was always so hard to pry off. My grandfather used to have to come into the kitchen and open it for her. He was a mechanic, so his hands were always so strong, but he could never get all the grease out from under his fingernails. No matter how much of that gritty orange soap he used, there was always a little bit left. But anyway, yeah, I just... I don't really have anything I look forward to anymore. It's just easier to come home and sit on the couch.
Would you say that your episodes of feeling down have ever been severe, or have they always been mild?

I feel like... didn't we just talk about this? Or maybe I just got off track earlier, I'm sorry. I really don't think it's ever been severe, honestly. It's just always been mild. Just that same flat feeling day in and day out. 

Speaking of flat, we actually had a pancake breakfast at school last Friday for the third graders. It was a fundraiser for the new playground equipment. The old swings are so rusted, you can hear them squeaking all the way from inside my classroom. I swear, that squeaking sound is worse than fingernails on a chalkboard. Not that we even have chalkboards anymore, thank goodness. The district replaced them all with those interactive smartboards three years ago. I still don't know how to use half the features on mine. Every time I try to show a science video, the sound cuts out, and the kids start getting so restless. Little Timmy—he sits in the front row—he always tries to come up and fix it for me. He's only eight, but he knows way more about computers than I do. His dad works in IT, I think. Or maybe he's an accountant? I can never remember. He always wears these really bright, loud patterned ties to parent-teacher conferences. Last time he wore one with tiny little golf clubs all over it. 

But anyway... what were you asking? Oh, right, the feeling down. No, it's never been severe. Just mild, I guess.
Have you experienced periods where you didn't feel this way at all over the past two years?

I don't think so... no. I can't really remember a time in the last couple of years where it went away. It's just been this constant sort of fog. 

Two years ago... gosh, that was the year the district decided to completely overhaul our math curriculum. What an absolute disaster that was. They brought in all these new textbooks right in the middle of October, and they were supposed to be this revolutionary new way of teaching fractions, but they didn't make any sense to the kids. Or to me, honestly. The parents were just furious. I had this one mother, Mrs. Gable—her son Matthew was a sweet boy, but very easily distracted—and she would call me almost every single night at 7 PM to complain about the homework. 7 PM! I'd be right in the middle of heating up my dinner, usually just opening a can of tomato soup or something because I'm too drained to cook, and my phone would just start ringing. 

I actually had to assign a special ringtone just for her so I'd know to brace myself. It sounded like one of those vintage telephones, you know, the heavy ones with the rotary dials? My aunt had one of those in her hallway when I was growing up. It was this hideous mustard yellow color, and the cord was so stretched out and tangled you could barely pull the receiver to your ear. She refused to replace it until it completely stopped working in, like, 1998. 

But, um... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, periods where I didn't feel this way. No, no breaks. Just the same feeling the whole time.
Have you ever had a period of time, say a few weeks or a couple of months, where you felt completely back to normal and didn't experience this flat feeling?

I really don't think so. I mean, like I said, it's just been this constant thing. I haven't had any weeks or months where I felt normal again. It's just always there. 

Speaking of months, though, we're coming up on the end of the semester, and it always feels like the longest month of the year. The kids get so antsy right before the winter break. We're trying to put together the holiday pageant, and it's just chaos. I volunteered to help with the costumes this year, which was probably a mistake. I'm supposed to be making tree costumes out of cardboard boxes for the kindergarteners. Have you ever tried to cut armholes in thick corrugated cardboard? It's impossible. I bought these special heavy-duty scissors from the craft store, the ones with the orange handles, but they barely make a dent. The lady at the checkout told me I should use a box cutter instead, but I'm terrified I'm going to slip and slice my finger open. My cousin Greg did that once when we were kids. We were trying to build a fort out of refrigerator boxes in my uncle's garage, and he was using this rusty old pocketknife. He had to get six stitches. The scar is still there, right across his thumb. He's a real estate agent now, sells these huge, fancy houses out in the suburbs. He's always posting pictures of these massive kitchens with marble countertops and double ovens. I don't know who needs two ovens, honestly. 

But anyway... sorry, I lost my train of thought. What was the question? Oh, right, feeling back to normal. No, I haven't had any time like that. Just the same flat feeling all the time.

patient.answer: I mean... no, not really. I try to think of something I want to do, and I just draw a blank. Even on the weekends, I wake up and I just... I don't really want to do anything. Which reminds me, I actually need to go to the grocery store this weekend because I'm completely out of coffee, and I cannot start my week without it. I usually go to the Trader Joe's on 4th Street, but the parking lot there is just a complete nightmare. It's so small, and people drive like maniacs trying to get a spot. Last time I was there, this guy in a massive SUV almost backed right into my sedan, and he didn't even look over his shoulder. I had to honk my horn for like ten seconds straight before he stopped.
